prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Husbands are allowed to slap their wives if they spend lavishly, a Saudi judge said recently during a seminar on domestic violence, Saudi media reported Sunday. It is OK to slap Saudi women who spend too much, a judge has told an audience. Arab News, a Saudi English-language daily newspaper based in Riyadh, reported that Judge Hamad Al-Razine said that "if a person gives SR 1,200 [$320] to his wife and she spends 900 riyals [$240] to purchase an abaya [the black cover that women in Saudi Arabia must wear] from a brand shop and if her husband slaps her on the face as a reaction to her action, she deserves that punishment." Women in the audience immediately and loudly protested Al-Razine's statement, and were shocked to learn the remarks came from a judge, the newspaper reported. Arab News reported that Al-Razine made his remark as he was attempting to explain why incidents of domestic violence had increased in Saudi Arabia. He said that women and men shared responsibility, but added that "nobody puts even a fraction of blame" on women, the newspaper said. Al-Razine "also pointed out that women's indecent behavior and use of offensive words against their husbands were some of the reasons for domestic violence in the country," it added. Domestic violence, which used to be a taboo subject in the conservative kingdom, has become a hot topic in recent years. Groups like the National Family Safety Program have campaigned to educate the public about the problem and help prevent domestic abuse. Saudi women's rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that Saudi women routinely face such attitudes. "This is how men in Saudi Arabia see women," she said in a telephone interview from the Saudi city of Dahran. "It's not something they read in a book or learned from a friend. They've been raised to see women this way, that they're less than a person." Al-Huwaider added that "I'm not surprised to see a judge or a religious man saying that - they've been raised in the same culture - a culture that tells them it's ok to raise your hand to a woman that this works." Another Saudi judge, in the city of Onaiza, was the source of a separate recent controversy: he twice denied a request from the mother of an 8-year-old girl that the girl be granted a divorce from her 47-year-old husband. Last month, after human-groups condemned the union, the girl was granted the divorce.

(CNN) — According to Saudi media reports on Sunday, a Saudi judge recently told a domestic violence seminar that husbands may slap their wives if the women spend money extravagantly.

Judge Hamad Al-Razine reportedly said it was acceptable for a Saudi woman to be slapped for excessive spending. Arab News, an English-language Saudi daily based in Riyadh, quoted him as saying that if a man gives his wife SR 1,200, or about $320, and she uses 900 riyals, around $240, to buy a designer abaya—the black garment women in Saudi Arabia are required to wear—then her husband’s response of slapping her in the face would be a punishment she deserved.

The newspaper said women attending the seminar reacted immediately with loud objections and were stunned that such comments had been made by a judge.

Arab News reported that Al-Razine made the comments while trying to discuss reasons for the rise in domestic violence cases in Saudi Arabia. He said both men and women bore responsibility, but claimed that “nobody puts even a fraction of blame” on women, according to the paper.

The report added that Al-Razine also cited what he described as women’s improper conduct and their use of insulting language toward their husbands as among the causes of domestic violence in the country.

In Saudi Arabia’s conservative society, domestic violence was once rarely discussed publicly, but in recent years it has become a widely debated issue. Organizations such as the National Family Safety Program have worked to raise public awareness and prevent abuse within families.

Saudi women’s rights campaigner Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that Saudi women regularly encounter such views. Speaking by telephone from Dahran, Saudi Arabia, she said, “This is how men in Saudi Arabia see women.” She added that these attitudes are not simply learned from books or friends, but are ingrained from upbringing, teaching men to regard women as “less than a person.”

Al-Huwaider said she was not surprised to hear such a statement from a judge or religious figure, because they had been brought up within the same culture—one that, she said, teaches that it is acceptable and effective to hit a woman.

A separate controversy recently involved another Saudi judge in the city of Onaiza. That judge twice rejected a mother’s request to obtain a divorce for her 8-year-old daughter from the girl’s 47-year-old husband. The divorce was granted last month after human rights groups condemned the marriage.

**Saudi judge’s comments on wife-slapping spark outrage among women’s rights advocates**

**Riyadh, Saudi Arabia** — A Saudi judge has drawn criticism from women’s rights activists after reportedly saying that husbands may slap their wives if they spend lavishly, remarks that have renewed debate over domestic violence and women’s legal protections in the kingdom.

The comments were made during a public discussion on domestic violence, according to local and international media reports. The judge suggested that excessive spending by wives could be one circumstance in which a husband might resort to striking his wife, citing an example in which a woman spends large sums of money on luxury goods.

Women’s rights advocates condemned the remarks, saying they risk legitimizing abuse and reinforcing social attitudes that make it harder for victims to report violence.

“No financial disagreement can justify physical violence,” said one Saudi women’s rights campaigner, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of criticizing judicial figures. “When such statements come from someone in authority, they can be used by abusive men to excuse their actions.”

Activists say domestic violence remains a serious problem in Saudi Arabia, where family matters are often treated as private and where victims may face social pressure not to report abuse. Although Saudi Arabia has introduced legal reforms in recent years, including measures aimed at protecting women from abuse, rights groups say enforcement can be inconsistent and victims may still struggle to access shelters, legal support and police protection.

Saudi Arabia passed a law criminalizing domestic abuse in 2013, setting penalties that can include imprisonment and fines. The government has also promoted hotlines and social services for abuse victims. But advocates argue that cultural stigma, guardianship-related practices and a lack of uniform enforcement continue to create barriers for women seeking help.

The judge’s reported remarks have also highlighted the broader debate over male authority within marriage in Saudi society. While the kingdom has eased some restrictions on women — including lifting the ban on women driving and expanding employment opportunities — human rights organizations say women still face discrimination in areas such as marriage, divorce, child custody and family law.

Some conservative commentators have defended the judge’s remarks as being taken out of context or as a reference to traditional interpretations of marital discipline. But activists say any suggestion that a husband has a right to strike his wife is incompatible with modern legal protections and international human rights standards.

“Domestic violence is not a private dispute or a disciplinary tool,” said another Gulf-based rights advocate. “It is abuse, and public officials should be sending a clear message that it is unacceptable under all circumstances.”

The controversy comes as Saudi Arabia continues to present itself as undergoing social reform under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda. Women’s rights campaigners acknowledge that some changes have improved daily life for many women, but they say deeper reforms are needed to ensure protection from violence and equality before the law.

For survivors of domestic abuse, advocates say the priority is not only legislation but also public messaging from courts, police and religious authorities.

“When authority figures speak clearly against violence, it helps victims come forward,” the Saudi campaigner said. “When they appear to justify it, victims are pushed back into silence.”

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia —** Remarks attributed to a Saudi judge suggesting that husbands may be justified in slapping wives in some circumstances have renewed debate over domestic abuse and judicial attitudes toward women in the kingdom, where activists say legal protections remain uneven despite recent reforms.

The controversy followed reports from a seminar on domestic violence in which a judge was quoted as saying that a husband might slap his wife if she spent money extravagantly. The comments drew criticism from women’s rights campaigners, who said they reflected a broader problem in how some courts and officials view violence within the family.

“This is the problem: they are always looking for excuses for men,” Saudi activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider said, criticizing the attitude that domestic violence can be justified as discipline. “Violence against women should never be accepted or explained away.”

Saudi Arabia has taken steps in recent years to address abuse, including public-awareness campaigns and mechanisms for reporting domestic violence. But rights advocates say women can still face social pressure, limited access to shelters, and difficulties navigating a justice system historically shaped by male guardianship norms and conservative interpretations of family law.

The debate has also revived memories of a child marriage case that caused international outrage when a Saudi court declined to immediately grant a divorce to a girl reported to be eight years old, who had been married to a man decades older. The judge’s handling of the case prompted criticism from human rights groups and Saudi activists, who argued that the girl’s welfare should have been the overriding concern. The case later became a focal point in calls for a legal minimum marriage age.

Saudi officials and religious authorities have at times defended the judiciary as independent and rooted in Islamic law, while also acknowledging the need to protect families from abuse. Some scholars and judges have rejected violence against women, saying Islamic principles require dignity and fairness within marriage.

Still, activists say individual cases show that women and girls remain vulnerable when judicial discretion is broad and legal standards are unclear.

“The issue is not only one judge or one case,” Al-Huwaider said. “It is whether women are treated as full human beings before the law.”

International rights organizations have urged Saudi Arabia to strengthen enforcement of domestic-abuse laws, set clear protections for minors, and ensure that judges and police treat violence against women as a crime rather than a private family matter.

The kingdom has introduced significant social changes in recent years, including allowing women to drive and expanding their participation in the workforce. But campaigners say family-law issues — including marriage, divorce, custody and abuse — remain a crucial test of whether reforms are changing women’s lives inside the home as well as in public.
